label: Hair loss
q: Is this scarring or non-scarring, and is it shedding or thinning?
lead: Two questions carry the whole differential. Are the follicular ostia still visible? If they have gone, the alopecia is scarring and the window to preserve hair is closing. And is the patient shedding hair or thinning without shedding? Those are different mechanisms with different investigations.

stop.l: Loss of follicular ostia — smooth, shiny scalp within the patch
stop.a: Cicatricial alopecia. The follicle is being destroyed and the loss is permanent. Biopsy the active edge now and start treatment before more is lost. Do not observe.

stop.l: Rapidly expanding patch with perifollicular erythema, scale and pain or burning
stop.a: Active lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus or folliculitis decalvans. Biopsy the advancing margin and treat urgently — this is an inflammatory emergency for the follicle.

stop.l: Boggy, tender, pustular scalp swelling with lymphadenopathy in a child
stop.a: Kerion. Systemic antifungal. Do not incise — it causes scarring, and the fluctuance is inflammatory rather than purulent.

stop.l: Diffuse hair loss with weight loss, fever or night sweats
stop.a: Investigate for systemic disease and malignancy. Anagen effluvium suggests cytotoxic exposure; diffuse loss with systemic features is not simple telogen effluvium.

stop.l: Moth-eaten patchy alopecia with a generalized rash or mucosal lesions
Boggy scalp nodules with interconnecting sinus tracts discharging pus in an adult
stop.a: Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp. This is a scarring alopecia, not a series of abscesses - repeated incision and antibiotics will not stop it and every month costs follicles. Start oral isotretinoin early, culture the drainage, and examine the axillae, groin and natal cleft for hidradenitis suppurativa and pilonidal disease.

dx.look: A neutrophilic scarring alopecia with follicular pustules, crusting and perifollicular erythema, healing with scarring and characteristic tufting - several hairs emerging from one dilated follicular opening (doll-hair) - most often on the vertex and occiput.
fr: Follicular pustules and crusting on a scarred scalp
Tufted hairs (several hairs from one follicle)
Loss of follicular openings (scarring)
Vertex and occiput
Staphylococcus aureus often cultured
dx.cf: Biopsy shows a neutrophilic then mixed folliculocentric infiltrate with scarring; swab pustules for S. aureus. As a scarring alopecia, treat early to preserve hair.
dx.dsc: Tufted follicular units (several hairs from one opening), perifollicular pustules, and follicular hyperkeratosis with loss of follicular openings.
dx.hp: A predominantly neutrophilic folliculocentric infiltrate at the infundibulum and isthmus progressing to perifollicular fibrosis and scarring, with tufting of adjacent follicles.
dx.assoc: Staphylococcus aureus is often implicated; it is a primary neutrophilic scarring alopecia, so early treatment preserves follicles.
dx.mgmt: Prolonged oral antistaphylococcal antibiotics (often doxycycline, or clindamycin plus rifampin) with topical or intralesional corticosteroids; culture-directed therapy and treat carriage.

dx.look: Rapid, extensive loss of growing (anagen) hairs days to weeks after an insult to the hair matrix - most often cytotoxic chemotherapy, but also radiation or toxic exposure; up to 80 to 90% of scalp hair can be shed.
fr: Rapid, extensive shedding within days to weeks of the insult
Recent chemotherapy, radiation or toxic exposure
Tapered or broken (dystrophic anagen) hairs
Loss far exceeding ordinary telogen shedding
Reversible when the insult stops
ag: Shedding 2 to 4 months after a trigger (telogen effluvium)
dx.cf: The temporal link to chemotherapy or another matrix insult is diagnostic; a hair pull yields dystrophic anagen hairs, and regrowth is expected once the insult ends.
dx.dsc: Dystrophic anagen hairs, tapered pencil-point and broken hairs, and black dots, with preserved follicular openings (non-scarring).
dx.hp: Matrix arrest with dystrophic anagen hairs on horizontal sections and no inflammation or scarring - a toxic, reversible process.
dx.assoc: Most often cytotoxic chemotherapy; the shedding is reversible when the insult stops, though regrowth may differ in color or texture, and scalp cooling can reduce chemotherapy-induced loss.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance and cosmetic support (wig, scalp cooling during chemotherapy); regrowth follows removal of the insult. Address any ongoing toxic exposure.

dx.look: Gradual, symmetric miniaturization. Men: bitemporal recession then vertex thinning (Hamilton). Women: diffuse widening of the central part with preservation of the frontal hairline (Ludwig). No shedding on hair pull. Variable shaft diameters on dermoscopy.
fr: Gradual over years, no dramatic shedding
Preserved frontal hairline in women, widening central part
Bitemporal and vertex pattern in men
Follicular ostia preserved
Miniaturized vellus hairs and diameter diversity on trichoscopy
Family history
dx.cf: Clinical, with trichoscopy showing hair diameter diversity over 20% and peripilar signs. Check ferritin, TSH and, in women with hirsutism or menstrual irregularity, androgens.
dx.dsc: Hair-shaft diameter diversity (over 20% variation) and follicular miniaturization, with a peripilar brown halo and increased vellus hairs, most marked over the vertex.
dx.hp: Increased telogen and miniaturized (vellus) follicles with a reduced terminal-to-vellus ratio (normally about 7:1, falling to 4:1 or less in androgenetic alopecia); sebaceous glands preserved and minimal inflammation on horizontal sections.
dx.assoc: In women with signs of hyperandrogenism (irregular menses, hirsutism), evaluate for PCOS or androgen excess; otherwise no work-up is needed.
dx.mgmt: Topical minoxidil (men and women) and oral finasteride or dutasteride in men (antiandrogens or spironolactone in women); low-level laser and hair transplantation as adjuncts.

dx.look: Sharply defined round or oval patches of complete hair loss with normal-appearing skin and preserved follicular ostia. Exclamation-mark hairs at the margins are diagnostic. Nail pitting in a fine hammered-brass pattern. Any hair-bearing site.
fr: Sharply circumscribed round or oval patches
Skin within the patch looks normal, ostia preserved
Exclamation-mark hairs at the active margin
Fine regular nail pitting
Personal or family autoimmune history, especially thyroid
Spontaneous regrowth of white hairs in some patches
ag: Broken hairs of differing lengths with an irregular outline
Scale and inflammation within the patch
dx.cf: Clinical, confirmed by exclamation-mark hairs and trichoscopy showing yellow dots, black dots and short vellus regrowth. Check thyroid function — autoimmune thyroiditis is the commonest association.
dx.dsc: Exclamation-mark hairs, black dots, yellow dots, tapered or broken hairs, and short regrowing vellus hairs within smooth patches.
dx.hp: A peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate (a swarm of bees) around anagen follicles with a shift toward catagen and telogen; non-scarring.
dx.assoc: Autoimmune thyroid disease, vitiligo, atopy and Down syndrome; screen only if symptoms suggest, since routine broad testing has little yield.
dx.mgmt: Intralesional triamcinolone (2-10 mg/mL) for limited patches; high-potency topical steroids as a safer first-line; topical immunotherapy or oral JAK inhibitors (for example baricitinib) for extensive disease.

dx.look: Diffuse shedding beginning 2–4 months after a trigger: childbirth, major illness, surgery, rapid weight loss, severe stress, or a new drug. The patient brings a bag of hair. Positive hair pull with 30–40 club hairs. No patches, no scarring, and full recovery is the rule.
fr: Abrupt diffuse shedding, patient can date its start
Identifiable trigger 2–4 months earlier
Positive hair pull yielding telogen club hairs
Diffuse, no discrete patches
Scalp looks normal
ag: Very gradual onset over years without shedding
dx.cf: Hair pull test with hair mount showing club-shaped telogen roots. Check ferritin, TSH, ANA and RPR. Reassure: complete regrowth is the rule, and reassurance is the main treatment.
dx.dsc: Numerous short upright regrowing hairs and empty follicles with preserved follicular openings; hair-diameter uniformity, unlike pattern loss.
dx.hp: Increased telogen follicles (over 15-20%) on horizontal sections with normal follicular architecture and no inflammation or scarring.
dx.assoc: A shedding response 2-4 months after a trigger - childbirth, illness or fever, surgery, rapid weight loss, thyroid disease, iron deficiency or a new drug; check ferritin and TSH.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance and correction of the trigger (iron, thyroid, nutrition); it is self-limited with full regrowth over months.

dx.look: Children predominantly. Scaly patches with broken-off hairs at varying lengths, black dots where hairs break at the surface, occipital lymphadenopathy, and in inflammatory forms a boggy tender kerion. Microsporum species fluoresce blue-green under a Wood lamp; Trichophyton does not.
fr: Child, particularly of African descent
Scale with broken hairs and black dots
Occipital or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
Boggy tender swelling in inflammatory forms
Household or classroom contacts, or an animal
ag: Complete smooth hair loss with normal scalp
dx.cf: KOH and fungal culture of plucked hairs and scale from the patch, collected with a brush or a moistened swab. Wood lamp is a screen, not an exclusion: Trichophyton tonsurans, the commonest cause in many populations, does not fluoresce.
dx.dsc: Comma hairs, corkscrew hairs and broken black-dot hairs with perifollicular scaling - characteristic of dermatophyte infection.
dx.hp: Fungal hyphae and spores within or around the hair shaft (PAS-positive); a suppurative folliculitis in kerion.
dx.assoc: Children, often of African descent; occipital or cervical lymphadenopathy is a useful clue. Confirm by KOH or culture, and examine and treat contacts and fomites.
dx.mgmt: An oral antifungal is required, since topicals do not penetrate the hair - griseofulvin or terbinafine; add a sporicidal shampoo (selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) to reduce spread.

dx.look: Bizarre, geometric or linear patches with an irregular outline, containing hairs broken at differing lengths and never completely bald. Usually on the side opposite the dominant hand, often the vertex or frontoparietal scalp. Eyebrows and lashes may be involved.
fr: Irregular, angulated, non-round outline
Hairs broken at varying lengths within the patch
Never completely bald
Eyelash or eyebrow involvement
Child or adolescent
ag: Perfectly round patches of complete loss
dx.cf: Trichoscopy shows broken hairs of differing lengths, flame hairs, V-sign and tulip hairs. Biopsy shows trichomalacia and pigment casts if confirmation is needed for a reluctant family. Handle the disclosure gently.
dx.dsc: Broken hairs of varying lengths, flame hairs, coiled hairs and V-signs within an irregular non-scarring patch; no exclamation-mark hairs or yellow dots.
dx.hp: A non-inflammatory catagen and telogen shift with pigment casts, trichomalacia and empty follicles - traumatic hair extraction without scarring.
dx.assoc: A body-focused repetitive behavior; screen for anxiety and OCD-spectrum disorders, and for a trichobezoar if hair is ingested. Bizarre, geometric or one-sided patterns are a clue.
dx.mgmt: Habit-reversal training and behavioral therapy first-line; N-acetylcysteine or an SSRI may help. Address the underlying psychological drivers.

dx.look: Hair loss along the frontal and temporal margins, matching the line of tension from braids, weaves, tight ponytails or a headscarf. The fringe sign — retained fine hairs at the frontal hairline in front of the area of loss — is characteristic. Reversible early, scarring if prolonged.
fr: Distribution matches the line of hair tension
Fringe sign: retained fine hairs anterior to the loss
History of braiding, weaving, extensions or tight styling
Perifollicular pustules or papules early
ag: Loss unrelated to any styling pattern
dx.cf: Clinical, from the pattern and the styling history. Biopsy only if scarring is established and the diagnosis is disputed. The therapeutic conversation about tension is more important than any test.
dx.dsc: Marginal hair loss with retained fringe hairs and, early, perifollicular erythema and hair casts; follicular openings are preserved until late.
dx.hp: Non-scarring early (reduced terminal follicles with preserved openings), becoming scarring if chronic - a preventable cicatricial alopecia.
dx.assoc: Chronic tension from tight braids, weaves, buns or extensions; the marginal fringe sign is characteristic and it is reversible if caught early.
dx.mgmt: Stopping the traction with looser styling is the essential step; topical minoxidil and intralesional steroids may help early; transplantation for established scarring.

dx.look: Perifollicular erythema and adherent perifollicular scale at the advancing margin, with progressive loss of follicular ostia leaving smooth, shiny, pale scarred scalp. Frontal fibrosing alopecia gives a band-like recession of the frontal and temporal hairline with eyebrow loss, typically in postmenopausal women. Itch, burning or tenderness.
fr: Perifollicular erythema and scale at the margin
Loss of follicular ostia — smooth shiny scalp
Band-like frontal hairline recession with eyebrow loss
Itch, burning or tenderness
Lichen planus elsewhere: skin, mouth or nails
dx.cf: Two 4 mm punch biopsies from the active margin, one sectioned transversely and one vertically, plus direct immunofluorescence. Biopsy the inflamed edge — the burnt-out center shows only fibrosis and answers nothing.
dx.dsc: Perifollicular scaling and erythema with loss of follicular openings; absent vellus hairs at the hairline in frontal fibrosing alopecia.
dx.hp: A lichenoid (interface) infiltrate targeting the follicular infundibulum and isthmus with perifollicular fibrosis - a scarring (cicatricial) alopecia; sample an active margin.
dx.assoc: A primary lymphocytic scarring alopecia; frontal fibrosing alopecia shows eyebrow loss and facial papules. Early diagnosis limits permanent loss.
dx.mgmt: Potent topical and intralesional corticosteroids to the active margin with hydroxychloroquine; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors for frontal fibrosing alopecia. The goal is to halt progression - lost hair does not regrow.

dx.n: Discoid lupus erythematosus of the scalp
dx.look: Well-demarcated plaques with follicular plugging, adherent scale, dyspigmentation — central hypopigmentation with a hyperpigmented rim — atrophy, telangiectasia and permanent scarring alopecia. Photodistributed, and often present on the face and ears too.
fr: Follicular plugging with adherent scale (carpet-tack sign)
Central hypopigmentation with a hyperpigmented border
Atrophy and telangiectasia within the patch
Involvement of ears, face or conchal bowl
Photosensitivity
dx.cf: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence showing interface dermatitis, follicular plugging and a positive lupus band. ANA and ENA, and assess for systemic disease.
dx.dsc: Follicular keratotic plugs, loss of follicular openings and thick arborizing vessels with pigment change in a scarred patch.
dx.hp: Interface dermatitis with follicular plugging, a superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal infiltrate, basement-membrane thickening and dermal mucin; direct immunofluorescence shows a lupus band.
dx.assoc: Check ANA and assess for systemic lupus (a minority progress); scarring alopecia is permanent, so treat early.
dx.mgmt: Photoprotection, potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids, and hydroxychloroquine first-line; advise smoking cessation, which improves antimalarial efficacy.

dx.look: Begins at the vertex or mid-scalp and expands centrifugally with a symmetric, smooth, shiny scarred center and preserved hair at the periphery. Predominantly in women of African descent. Tenderness, itch or tingling often precede visible loss.
fr: Vertex or crown onset, expanding centrifugally
Symmetric, smooth, shiny scarred center
Woman of African descent
Tenderness, itching or tingling
History of heat, chemical relaxers or traction
ag: Frontal hairline recession as the dominant feature
dx.cf: Biopsy from the expanding margin. Premature desquamation of the inner root sheath is characteristic. Early treatment preserves the follicles that remain — by the time the center is smooth, that hair is gone.
dx.dsc: A peripilar white-gray halo with loss of follicular openings, spreading centrifugally from the crown and vertex.
dx.hp: Premature desquamation of the inner root sheath with perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation and concentric lamellar fibrosis - a scarring alopecia; biopsy an active margin.
dx.assoc: Most common in women of African descent; traction and heat or chemical styling are debated contributors. Early treatment preserves follicles.
dx.mgmt: Stop damaging hair practices; potent topical and intralesional corticosteroids with oral doxycycline (anti-inflammatory); the goal is to halt progression.

dx.look: Patchy, irregular, moth-eaten alopecia of the scalp, beard or eyebrows, accompanying a generalized non-pruritic eruption with lymphadenopathy. Non-scarring and fully reversible with treatment.
fr: Moth-eaten irregular patchy loss
Concurrent non-pruritic generalized eruption
Palms and soles involved
Generalized lymphadenopathy
Sexual risk history
ag: Isolated hair loss with no rash and no lymphadenopathy
dx.cf: Treponemal test with RPR titer. Offer HIV testing. The alopecia resolves entirely with treatment.
dx.dsc: Preserved follicular ostia with patchy incomplete thinning rather than total loss, scattered black dots and yellow dots, and short hypopigmented vellus hairs. Exclamation-mark hairs and tapered dystrophic hairs are absent, which is what separates it from alopecia areata.
dx.hp: A perifollicular plasma-cell-rich lymphocytic infiltrate with a shift of follicles into telogen; spirochetes on immunostain.
dx.assoc: Moth-eaten non-scarring alopecia as a sign of secondary syphilis - send treponemal and non-treponemal serology, and offer HIV testing.
dx.mgmt: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly (doxycycline if penicillin-allergic and not pregnant); the alopecia regrows after treatment. Notify partners.

dx.look: Deep, boggy, fluctuant nodules over the vertex and occiput that coalesce and interconnect through sinus tracts, expressing pus on pressure and healing with hypertrophic and keloidal scarring. Predominantly young men of African descent. Often accompanied by acne conglobata and hidradenitis suppurativa - the follicular occlusion syndrome.
fr: Boggy fluctuant nodules that interconnect beneath the scalp
Sinus tracts discharging pus on pressure
Vertex and occiput
Young man, most often of African descent
Coexisting acne conglobata, hidradenitis suppurativa or pilonidal sinus
Repeated courses of antibiotics with only temporary benefit
ag: A single flat patch of normal-looking skin
dx.cf: Clinical, from boggy interconnecting nodules and sinus tracts on the vertex and occiput. Swab pustules and sinus drainage for Staphylococcus aureus, and biopsy only if the diagnosis is disputed. Treat it as a scarring alopecia from the first visit - the sinuses destroy follicles while it is being managed as recurrent abscesses.
dx.dsc: Yellow structureless areas with three-dimensional yellow dots, black dots and broken hairs over a boggy surface, with complete loss of follicular openings in burnt-out areas.
dx.hp: Follicular plugging with suppurative follicular and perifollicular abscesses and a mixed infiltrate, progressing to foreign-body giant cells, granulation tissue and scarring with epithelialized sinus tracts.
dx.assoc: Part of the follicular occlusion syndrome with acne conglobata, hidradenitis suppurativa and pilonidal sinus; Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent secondary colonizer and should be documented and treated. Longstanding disease carries a small squamous cell carcinoma risk.
dx.mgmt: Oral isotretinoin is the most effective agent and should be started early; add antistaphylococcal antibiotics guided by culture, intralesional corticosteroids, and drainage of fluctuant areas. TNF inhibitors or wide excision with grafting for refractory disease.

dx.look: Firm follicular papules and pustules on the occipital scalp and nape that coalesce into a horizontal keloidal band or plaque, with tufted hairs emerging through it and permanent hair loss above and within it. Almost exclusively men of African descent, aggravated by close clipping, shaving and shirt-collar friction.
fr: Occipital scalp and nape of the neck
Firm follicular papules coalescing into a keloidal band
Man of African descent
Close clipping, shaving or collar friction
Follicular pustules and tufted hairs within the keloidal tissue
Loss of follicular openings within the band
dx.cf: Clinical, from the site and the keloidal morphology. Swab pustules for Staphylococcus aureus. Biopsy is rarely needed - the horizontal keloidal band at the nape is characteristic, and early treatment prevents the plaque stage.
dx.dsc: Follicular pustules and tufted hairs emerging through firm white keloidal tissue with absent follicular openings at the nape, and no perifollicular scaling.
dx.hp: Perifollicular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation at the level of the isthmus with follicular destruction, naked hair shafts in the dermis with a foreign-body reaction, and dense dermal fibrosis becoming frankly keloidal in older lesions.
dx.assoc: Occurs almost exclusively in men of African descent and is aggravated by close haircuts, shaving and collar friction. Staphylococcus aureus should be documented on culture and treated. Frequently coexists with pseudofolliculitis barbae.
dx.mgmt: Stop close clipping and reduce collar friction - this is the essential step. Intralesional triamcinolone and potent topical corticosteroids for early papules, topical clindamycin or an oral tetracycline for pustules, and surgical excision with healing by secondary intention for established keloidal plaques.

dx.n: Hair shaft disorder (trichorrhexis nodosa, monilethrix, loose anagen syndrome)
dx.look: Hair that will not grow long rather than hair that falls out. The scalp is normal and the follicular openings are preserved; the shaft itself is at fault. Trichorrhexis nodosa gives white nodes along the shaft that fracture like two brooms pushed together, monilethrix gives regularly beaded shafts with keratosis pilaris of the nape, and loose anagen syndrome gives a toddler with sparse fine hair that pulls out painlessly.
fr: Hair will not grow long, with little true shedding
Normal scalp with preserved follicular openings
Shafts break in the mid-length rather than coming away at the root
Chemical relaxing, bleaching, perming, heat or vigorous brushing
Sparse fine hair in a young child that extracts painlessly
Keratosis pilaris of the nape and family history in monilethrix
ag: Discrete round patches of complete loss
An identifiable trigger 2 to 4 months before an abrupt shedding
dx.cf: Light microscopy of a hair mount is the diagnosis and takes minutes. Trichorrhexis nodosa shows paintbrush fractures at white nodes, monilethrix shows regular beading with internodal constrictions, and loose anagen syndrome yields anagen hairs with ruffled cuticles and no root sheath after a painless pull.
dx.dsc: Beaded or nodular shafts with paintbrush fractures and short broken hairs of even caliber, over a normal scalp with preserved follicular openings and no yellow dots or perifollicular scale.
dx.hp: Rarely biopsied - the abnormality is in the shaft, not the follicle, and horizontal sections are normal in acquired breakage. Loose anagen syndrome shows anagen follicles with a defective inner root sheath.
dx.assoc: Acquired trichorrhexis nodosa follows chemical and thermal trauma; it is also a marker of Netherton syndrome and argininosuccinic aciduria. Monilethrix is autosomal dominant. Loose anagen syndrome affects fair-haired young children and improves with age.
dx.mgmt: Stop the traumatic practice - relaxers, bleaching, perming, heat styling and hard brushing - and use gentle conditioning care with wide-tooth combs and protective styling. Congenital forms need genetic counseling and time rather than a drug; loose anagen syndrome resolves spontaneously.

dx.look: Discrete, smooth, skin-colored or faintly pink irregular patches of hair loss with absent follicular openings and no scale, no crust and no perifollicular erythema. Early patches are moth-eaten and coalesce into larger areas with islands of surviving hair - the footprints-in-the-snow pattern. It is the burnt-out end stage of several scarring alopecias.
fr: Smooth, shiny, irregular patches with absent follicular openings
No scale, crust or perifollicular erythema anywhere
Coalescence into a footprints-in-the-snow pattern
Islands of surviving hair within the affected area
Slowly progressive over years without symptoms
ag: Active perifollicular erythema and adherent scale
Normal-looking skin with preserved follicular openings
dx.cf: A diagnosis of exclusion. Biopsy any residual active edge, with vertical and transverse sections plus direct immunofluorescence, chiefly to exclude lichen planopilaris and discoid lupus - a wholly burnt-out patch shows only fibrous tracts and cannot name a cause.
dx.dsc: Irregular ivory-white areas with complete loss of follicular openings, no perifollicular scaling and no erythema, containing residual islands of normal terminal hairs.
dx.hp: Early lesions show perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation with concentric fibrosis, indistinguishable from lichen planopilaris; late lesions show only fibrous tracts with loss of follicles and sebaceous glands.
dx.assoc: Regarded as the end stage of noninflammatory and previously inflammatory scarring alopecias rather than a disease of its own. The value of the label is prognostic - the loss is permanent and the aim is to halt any residual activity.
dx.mgmt: Potent topical and intralesional corticosteroids with hydroxychloroquine while any activity remains; if the process has been stable for a year or more, hair transplantation or scalp reduction can be considered.

dx.look: A triangular or lance-shaped area of hair loss over the frontotemporal scalp with its base at the hairline, present from birth or noticed in the first few years. It is not truly bald: fine vellus hairs fill the patch, follicular openings are preserved, and the size and shape do not change over a lifetime. Unilateral in most.
fr: Frontotemporal triangular or lance-shaped patch with its base at the hairline
Present from birth or the first years of life
Fine vellus hairs within the patch rather than complete baldness
Unchanged in size and shape over years
Follicular openings preserved, skin otherwise normal
dx.cf: Clinical, from the site, the shape and the lifelong stability, confirmed by trichoscopy showing a field of vellus hairs surrounded by normal terminal hairs. No investigation is needed. The purpose of making the diagnosis is to stop repeated intralesional steroid injections for a misdiagnosis of alopecia areata.
dx.dsc: A sharply bounded triangular field of fine vellus hairs among normal terminal hairs, with preserved follicular openings and none of the yellow dots, black dots or exclamation-mark hairs of alopecia areata.
dx.hp: Normal follicular density with terminal follicles replaced by vellus follicles; no inflammation, no miniaturization gradient and no fibrosis.
dx.assoc: Isolated in most; occasional association with Down syndrome and phakomatosis pigmentovascularis. Its importance is that it is repeatedly mistaken for alopecia areata and injected or treated for years without effect.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance - it is stable, benign and permanent. No medical treatment works. Hair transplantation or excision of the patch if the cosmetic impact matters.

ctx.s: Tinea capitis is predominantly pediatric, Fitzpatrick 8e §26
Frontal fibrosing alopecia occurs predominantly in postmenopausal women, Fitzpatrick 8e §31

ctx.l: Major illness, surgery, childbirth or weight loss 2–4 months ago
New drug in the last 6 months
Personal or family autoimmune disease, especially thyroid
Braiding, weaving, extensions or chemical relaxers
Known lichen planus of skin, mouth or nails
Sexual risk exposure in the last 12 months
Man of African descent who wears his hair close-clipped or shaved
Coexisting acne conglobata, hidradenitis suppurativa or pilonidal sinus
Chemical relaxing, bleaching, perming or frequent heat styling

find.l: Follicular ostia are absent — scalp smooth and shiny
find.s: Loss of follicular ostia defines cicatricial alopecia, Fitzpatrick 8e §31

find.l: Perifollicular erythema and adherent scale at the margin
Sharply defined round or oval patch, skin looks normal
Exclamation-mark hairs at the margin
Fine regular nail pitting (hammered brass)
Positive hair pull — more than 6 hairs come away easily
find.s: Normally 3–5 hairs are dislodged; more suggests pathology, Fitzpatrick 8e §31

find.l: Patient can date the sudden onset of shedding
Gradual thinning over years with no shedding phase
Widened central part with a preserved frontal hairline
Band-like recession of the frontal hairline with eyebrow loss
Scale with broken hairs and black dots
Occipital or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
Irregular geometric patch with hairs broken at varying lengths
Loss follows the line of hair tension, with a retained fringe
find.s: Fringe sign in traction alopecia, Fitzpatrick 8e §31

find.l: Follicular plugging with central hypopigmentation and atrophy
Moth-eaten patchy loss with a generalized rash
Itch, burning or tenderness in the affected scalp
find.s: Symptoms suggest active follicular inflammation, Fitzpatrick 8e §31

find.l: Follicular pustules with tufted hairs on a scarred scalp
Extensive rapid shedding within weeks of chemotherapy
Boggy fluctuant scalp nodules with interconnecting sinus tracts that discharge pus
Firm follicular papules coalescing into a keloidal band at the nape and occiput
Hair breaks along its length and will not grow long, over a normal scalp
Sparse fine hair in a young child that extracts easily and painlessly
Scarred patches with no scale, crust or perifollicular erythema anywhere
find.s: Absence of inflammation in an established scarring alopecia, Fitzpatrick 8e §31

find.l: Coalescing irregular bald patches with islands of surviving hair (footprints in the snow)
Triangular frontotemporal patch of fine vellus hairs present since childhood
The area of loss has not changed in size or shape for years
find.s: Calibrated estimate - stability separates congenital patterning from active alopecia

find.l: Extracted hairs show tapered dystrophic (pencil-point) roots rather than club-shaped telogen bulbs
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §31 - anagen effluvium sheds dystrophic anagen hairs, telogen effluvium sheds club hairs

test.w: Every case of hair loss, before anything else. It answers the scarring question in seconds by showing whether follicular ostia are present.
test.p: Yellow and black dots with short vellus regrowth support alopecia areata. Hair diameter diversity over 20% supports pattern hair loss. Perifollicular scale with absent ostia indicates a cicatricial process. Comma and corkscrew hairs indicate tinea capitis.
test.n: A normal trichoscopic pattern in genuine shedding supports telogen effluvium, which has no specific scalp findings.
test.x: Trichoscopy replaces a great deal of biopsy in this presentation. Absent ostia is the single finding that converts an outpatient review into an urgent one.

test.l: Hair pull test with hair mount
test.w: Any complaint of shedding. Grasp about 50 hairs and pull gently and steadily.
test.p: More than 6 hairs, with club-shaped telogen roots on mounting, confirms an effluvium. Look for the trigger 2–4 months back.
test.n: A negative pull in a patient reporting shedding suggests the effluvium has ended, or that the problem is thinning rather than shedding.
test.x: Ask when the hair was last washed. Washing within 24 hours markedly reduces the yield and produces a false negative.

test.l: KOH and fungal culture of plucked hairs and scale
test.w: Any scaly patchy hair loss in a child, and in an adult with scale and broken hairs.
test.p: Confirms and speciates. Tinea capitis requires systemic therapy — topical treatment does not reach the follicle. Screen and treat household contacts.
test.n: Does not exclude if the patient has been pretreated. Repeat off treatment.
test.x: Collect with a toothbrush or moistened swab over the patch — better yield, and far more acceptable to a child than plucking. A Wood lamp is a screening aid only: Trichophyton tonsurans does not fluoresce and is the commonest cause in many populations.

test.l: Two 4 mm punch biopsies from the active margin
test.w: Any alopecia where follicular ostia are lost. Urgently — destroyed follicles do not return.
test.p: Lymphocytic perifollicular inflammation at the isthmus with concentric fibrosis indicates lichen planopilaris. Interface change with follicular plugging and a positive lupus band indicates discoid lupus. Neutrophilic infiltrate suggests folliculitis decalvans.
test.n: A burnt-out center shows only fibrosis and cannot distinguish the causes. That is a sampling failure, not a result.
test.x: Biopsy the inflamed advancing margin, never the smooth center. Send one specimen for transverse sectioning and one for vertical, and add direct immunofluorescence.

test.l: Ferritin, TSH, ANA and treponemal serology
test.w: Diffuse shedding or diffuse thinning without patches.
test.p: Iron deficiency, thyroid disease, lupus or syphilis, each of which is reversible, and each of which is regularly missed in a patient labeled as having simple telogen effluvium.
test.n: Normal results in a patient with an identified trigger support telogen effluvium and permit confident reassurance — complete regrowth is the rule.
test.x: Serum iron alone is not adequate; ferritin is the relevant measure, and many clinicians aim above 30–50 µg/L in hair loss even where the laboratory reference range extends lower.

test.l: Androgen profile: total and free testosterone, DHEAS
test.w: Female pattern hair loss with hirsutism, acne, menstrual irregularity or rapid progression.
test.p: Raised androgens suggest polycystic ovary syndrome, adrenal hyperplasia, or rarely a tumor. Refer to endocrinology.
test.n: Most women with pattern hair loss have normal androgens. A normal result does not exclude the diagnosis or preclude antiandrogen treatment.
test.x: Do not order this reflexively in every woman with thinning hair. Reserve it for those with other signs of hyperandrogenism.

test.l: Light microscopy of a hair mount
test.w: Hair that breaks or will not grow long over a normal scalp, and any child with sparse fine hair. Cut or gently pluck 20 to 30 hairs, mount them in mounting medium and read them under low power.
test.p: Paintbrush fractures at white nodes indicate trichorrhexis nodosa. Regular beading with internodal constrictions indicates monilethrix. Anagen hairs with ruffled cuticles and no root sheath after a painless pull indicate loose anagen syndrome. Club-shaped telogen roots instead point back to an effluvium.
test.n: Normal shafts redirect the assessment to a cycling or follicular disorder - repeat the trichoscopy and look again for miniaturization, patches and loss of follicular openings.
test.x: The commonest error is not looking. Breakage is recorded as shedding, the ferritin and TSH come back normal, and the styling history that caused it is never taken. Cut the hairs rather than plucking them when assessing breakage, or the fracture pattern is destroyed.

test.l: Swab of pustules and sinus drainage for culture and sensitivities
test.w: Any pustular or discharging scalp lesion before starting antibiotics, in dissecting cellulitis, folliculitis decalvans and acne keloidalis alike.
test.p: Staphylococcus aureus is common and should be treated on sensitivities, including nasal decolonization. It does not settle whether the organism is the primary driver or a colonizer, and it does not remove the need for anti-inflammatory and antifollicular occlusion therapy.
test.n: A negative culture does not exclude a neutrophilic scarring alopecia and does not justify withholding treatment. These conditions are follicular occlusion and inflammation first, infection second.
test.x: The trap is treating a positive culture as the whole diagnosis. Repeated antibiotic courses for a boggy scalp with sinuses lose follicles month by month - the decision that matters is starting isotretinoin, not the choice of antibiotic.

test.l: Scalp biopsy of a burnt-out patch with elastic tissue stain
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin; calibrated estimate
test.w: Established scarring alopecia with no clinical inflammation, where the cause has never been established and treatment decisions depend on it.
test.p: Fibrous tracts with loss of follicles and sebaceous glands, with no lichenoid interface change, no lupus band and no neutrophils, supports pseudopelade of Brocq as an end-stage process. Elastic staining helps separate the wedge-shaped elastic loss of lichen planopilaris from the preserved pattern of discoid lupus.
test.n: A specific pattern - lichenoid interface change, a positive lupus band, or a neutrophilic infiltrate - names the underlying disease and takes precedence over the pseudopelade label.
test.x: Sampling error dominates. Take the specimen from any residual pink or slightly raised edge, not from the smooth center, and send one for transverse sectioning and one for vertical with direct immunofluorescence. A center-only biopsy answers nothing and is often reported as pseudopelade by default.

flag: Look for follicular ostia with a dermatoscope before anything else. If they are gone, the alopecia is scarring, biopsy is urgent, and every week of delay costs follicles that will not come back.
